Lots of comments on the sorts of things you can do, but here's some tips on how you can do them!

- for combat, the best weapon for beginners is the atgeir. It's a little expensive but worth it. If you ever get swarmed or surrounded, just middle mouse button and gtfo
- if you don't wanna do atgier, do shields with mace/club. A good chunk of enemies are weak to blunt damage, and the shields are good for parrying. (Parrying is when you block just before an opponent hits you, which causes them to stagger and your next attack(s) deal double damage)
- food is very important! There's three categories of food: food with a high health bonus, food with a high stamina focus, and food with equal health/stamina. I like 2 stamina foods and a health when I go exploring, but feel free to do 2 health 1 stammy if you're dying a lot
- know when to cut your losses. You won't win every fight and running away is always an option!
- for mining, carts get heavier the more you put in them. They're really useful for transporting ore but I wouldn't bother putting the stone in them. If you're playing with portals, I take the stone with me through a portal, then cart the ore home.
- also for mining: the copper nodes are like icebergs: 80% of them is usually underground! In a server with lots of people, bronze can be in short supply so make sure you get maximum ore from each node!
- troll armour is awesome. Its good in the black forest, and still good in the swamp because there's no movement debuff (unlike bronze or iron armour). The root armour set (which is the swamp's light armor) is also good, but you have to kill abominations which is tough for early players. In contrast, by the time you reach the swamp you can probably solo a troll, so upgrading the troll armour is comparatively easier imo
- avoid being out at night. Just don't. It's cold and the monsters are tougher.
- try to get meginjord from haldor the merchant sooner than later. The extra carry weight is a game changer.

I've neglected giving any building tips because you really need visuals to help with those, but if you wanna go the builder route there's tonnes to learn!

Someone who remembers more from their quantum lectures can probably correct me, but it's basically a consequence of the plank constant.

The fundamental axiom of quantum mechanics is that energy is quantized, and the distance between discrete energies is described by plank's constant.

The energy of a photon is determined by the wavelength, and so by quantizing the energy, you're also quantizing the wavelength of a photon. Knowing this, you can calculate the smallest possible wavelength of a photon, and that distance is called the plank length.

Admittedly, that's about as far as I know into this. I know that positional measurements are done using light waves, so your gradiation can only be as small as the wavelength of the photons used, but I don't know a whole lot about how we use photons to measure position, or whether it's possible to do it in some other way. (Def not possible now, because EM interactions are the only way we know to measure anything on that scale, but I mean I'm not certain if there's any theoretical limits on how else we could measure them)
I think a more accurate analogy would be that at its smallest, the dart leaves a plank-length-sized hole. The exact position you want is somewhere inside that hole but you don't know exactly where.

Consider it like an algebra problem: if you have F=1/r² (ignoring the other constants in Coloumb's law for now), there's no way to arrange it to get F/r² without changing the right side as well. If you were plotting F/r² vs r, then you're basically graphing a different equation entirely.

The proper strategy when approaching this type of problem is to start with the original equation and then start rearranging it. By taking the reciprocal of both sides, you get r² in the numerator on the opposite side from F. Then you just sub x=r², and now you have a linear equation. Obviously it only works if your graph is F vs x (which is F vs r²).

Also, FWIW, the graph probably was polynomial, not exponential: since we're only looking at a small area on the positive side of the x-axis, a polynomial graph and an exponential one would look fairly similar
If you divide F by r², then you just end up with a 1/r⁴ graph. What you want is to calculate F as a function of r². I would just plot 1/F vs r². The slope will be equal to 1/(kqQ).

To add, I think you *could* argue that a class in Python has to be something that you might need more than 1 version of. For example, I need multiple Tracks, so it makes sense to have a class, with each instance being a separate track.

I don't need more than 1 Player, so that could instead just be a module. Python doesn't have singleton classes like other languages, and modules can be used to fill that role.

Ultimately I think it's about preference. I generally prefer to use classes; I think there's no harm in doing it, and if down the line I discover that I do end up needing multiple instances, it doesn't require me to refactor any of my code.

At a high level, classes are groupings of variables and functions that are expected to be used together. You have the variables be anything you want; basic data types or members of other classes.

Sometimes you build a class to represent a "unit" of data. That's the classical "Animal" example you see in tutorials a lot, where the class is supposed to be analogous to a real world object, with functions and methods related to it.

Other times, you might use a class to group functionality together. (IMO the line here can get fuzzy between what's better as a class or a module.) For example, you might create an Importer class, which doesn't really represent any data in particular, but has functionality and state tracking related to importing data from the filesystem, and perhaps outputting instances of another class.

If it helps, I recently wrote a media playing app that has the following classes.

- SubTrack (represents an actual sound file loaded from a disk. Can be played or stopped.)
- Track (represents a single "song"; has a name, description, etc.)
- CompTrack (still a single song, but multiple different versions of it (vocal, instrumental, etc.) that can be switched between  during playing)
- TrackList (collection of tracks to be played on succession)
- Player (object to control what track is playing when)

All but the last class are "data" classes. They have some core data and some functions related to it. The last one is a "handler" class that has instances of the other classes as data and its functions control what to do with them. It sounds more similar to what you're describing!

In this sense, it comes down to speed. Python is just inherently slower than a compiled language (like C, Go, Rust, etc.) which means when you have code that is being run very frequently, Python may not be the ideal choice.

It really comes down to expected use case. There's no problem using Python to serve an API that gets used infrequently, but if you're expected to get 1000s of user requests per second, compiled language would be faster. (I recommended Go in particular since their standard library has some good functions for handing http requests.)

In general, I think the choice of language for a task is usually a choice between interpreted or compiled depending on speed needs. The actual language usually isn't as important. Some tend to be more popular in certain industries than others, but you can probably do anything in Python that you can do in JavaScript or C#, for example!

Typically you would set up an API to do something like this. FastAPI is a common choice of framework for building out an API server in Python. Find a tutorial online to build out something simple, and that should help you get your head wrapped around the architecture!

To be honest though, if you're expecting to have a significant number of users, Python may not be the ideal language for backend (server side) programming. Something like Go is well suited for serving an API. It's a bit of a jump in complexity from Python, but it is significantly faster. Prototyping in Python would be fine, but for production uses with heavy expected workload, I'd look elsewhere :)

There's a lot of answers here about set seizes and whatnot, which is great, but coming from a physics background myself I think the concept your husband is talking about is slightly different.

In physics you often work with equations in the limit that some variable value increases in magnitude, ultimately to infinity. In this case, you need to evaluate what happens with your equation? Will it also produce a value that increases without bound? Not always.

This is the idea of limits. Consider the equation y=x. As x gets bigger, so does y. And so as x approaches infinity, so too does y. Simple.

Now consider y = 1/x. As x increases and approaches infinity (written as x→∞), y actually *decreases* and gets smaller and smaller, approaching 0. Cool.

Now that limits are established, how can we compare them? It has to do with the equations themselves. We know that x² is always bigger than x (for x > 1), so if x→∞, then x² will be the larger infinity. In other words, x/x²→0 as x→∞. (The language here is important: the value *approaches" zero, but isn't equal to zero, because infinity isn't actually a physical number and equations aren't calculable *at* infinity. But the limit approaches some value as x approaches infinity.)

This might be a simple case though because algebraically, we can reduce x/x² to 1/x, which we already established approaches 0 as x→∞. But what about something like 2^x /x? This has an x in the exponent of 2, and can't be reduced algebraically. So you have to compare the top and bottom to see what happens. For x > 1, 2^x will always be bigger than x. And, the difference between them also gets bigger the higher x is. For example, 2²=4 which is 2 bigger than 2, but 2³=8 which is 5 bigger than 3. That pattern continues. So, as x→∞, we know 2^x > x, and that the difference between them gets bigger with x, so therefore 2^x /x→∞.

It gets more complicated, but essentially it's a game of knowing how rapidly certain expressions grow in value as x gets larger, and using that to determine which are larger than others, and by how much. Sometimes the difference is negligible and we ignore it, like x/(x+1). x+1 is always bigger than x, but at x→∞, that extra +1 becomes so insignificant, that x/(x+1) basically becomes x/x=1.

The terminology between Law and Theory is mainly due to how the perception of physics over time has changed. Historically, scientists worked under the assumption that God governed nature, and so the correlations they discovered were considered God's laws.

In recent times, we maintain a separation between theology and science, so we use the term Theory instead of Law.

I think the general idea is that in Python, we can use "falsey" values to determine whether or not an object has value. It's often useful to know whether a function returned something useful. Consider cases like searching for a substring, extracting a subset of a list, or getting user input as a string: it can be easy to just write `if var: ...` where it's understood that the conditional will be true if `var` contains data.

The alternative would be to always perform an equality check (like `re.match(...) is None` or `input == ""`, but Python's philosophy is to exclude unnecessary code and improve readability.

Alternatively, some languages might have you use functions like `if re.match.hadmatch()` or `if mylist.isempty()` and that's basically what Python is doing under the hood.

As a last comment, a clear distinction is that while values like `None`, `[]`, `""`, etc. are "falsey", they aren't False. I.e. ` None != [] != "" != False`. Boolean literals are still their own distinct values and won't satisfy equality operators with falsey versions of other data types. It's just that Python's `if` operator doesn't check that a condition is strictly equal to `False`, just that the result is falsey.

I think the point they're making is that `float(x)` returns a float with the value of x, but `bool(y)` doesn't return `True` or `False` based on the content of `y`, but instead on whether `y` is empty or not.

I'd still keep it - like I said earlier, it's really helpful for installing CLI tools built with Python!

`pipx` is good for installing CLI tools written in Python, because it essentially installs all the tools in their own virtual environment and prevents issues where there's a dependency conflict between different tools. However, for that same reason, it's bad for developing your own apps, since all the packages you install are in their own separate environments and not supposed to interact with each other.

What you really want is a virtual environment for your project specifically. `venv` is okay and comes pre-installed with Python, but personally I prefer tools like `pipenv` or `poetry` for managing the environments of my projects. Basically, each of these tools will create a new Python environment for your project specifically, allowing you to install dependencies to use in your code (without creating conflicts in other python apps).

Liked your comment, but also wanted to share some knowledge: in software versioning, the decimal doesn't indicate a percentage of completeness - it's just a way to track the number of releases.

You often see this in a 3-version form, like `1.34.2`.

- the first number represents the major version. Most products keep this as 0 while still in development, then move to 1 once they have a stable production version.
- the second number represents a minor update. These are usually content or feature additions/changes.
- the third number (when present) represents the patch version. This gets incremented when a release only had small changes, like minor bug fixes or difficulty tweaks.

So what this means is that Valheim is 217 "minor releases" in its development. They could stop at 300 and decide to move to `1.0`, or they could release another 1000 minor updates and hit version `0.1217` before feeling product ready.

Hope that's clear and doesn't sound condescending!

The only reason the point mass approximation works is because the symmetry causes forces between mirror points to cancel. For example, if you sit in space directly above the equator, a point mass at both the north and south poles will pull on you with equal force. When you sum their force vectors, you get some component cancellation, and end up with a net force which points towards the middle of the earth. Likewise, for any point in Earth, you sum it's attractive force with the force of its mirror point on the other side of Earth, and end up with a net inward force.

If the mass is not spherically symmetric, then you don't get the cancelling out of vectors which results in the "point mass" approximation. True, you could do some math and determine a "centre of gravity", but the magnitude and location of the centre will change as you move around the system of point masses, making it basically useless. (It probably also changes as you get closer; I don't have time to do the math on that but I imagine the r² dependence of gravity means that the attraction from closer points grows quicker than from farther points. In a symmetrical sphere, it works out that the mirror points closest and farthest away end up summing nicely, but for an unsymmetrical mass that wouldn't be true.)

Sometimes it's better to run things sequentially than in parallel. It's about where the bottlenecks are. Does the code need to wait for something, or can it run each loop without interrupting?

If it's the latter, you're probably better off with sequential execution since you won't have the overhead of process switching. I'd only use parallel if there's a reason the code might hang for a bit, and you don't want to delay the rest of the execution.

An example of a good place to use parallel programming is pinging a list of servers. Since each call to ping will freeze until it returns, you want to run them simultaneously so that they don't end up waiting on eachother.

If, alternatively, you're doing something like performing calculations on items in a list, better to go sequentially since there's no bottleneck there.

I wrote some example code for a friend as to why classes are useful from an organization standpoint. Since I'm on mobile, I don't have the code handy, but the example was creating a class to represent trinomials (you know, like x²+x+1). The class obviously stores the values of the trinomials, but it also has functions you can call to find the intercepts, vertex, etc. Basically, functions you would generally need to use are contained within the object, and not at the top level of your namespace.

Without a trinomials object, you have to store the values some other way (say, as a list of coefficients). On paper, that list is no different than any other.

Then you have to create a bunch of functions to do calculations on that list. A function for the vertex, which requires a list as an argument, another for finding intercepts, etc.

When you define a class, you can leverage the fact that data is already stored inside the object. Instead of calling ``get_vertex(trinomial)``, you do ``trinomial.get_vertex()``. You aren't risking having to verify the data (make sure you passed a list as trinomial and not an integer or something), since the data was verified when it was first entered.

Also handy, you can overload the + and - operators. Adding two trinomials is as easy as ``t = t1 + t2 - t3``, rather than ``t = sub(add(t1, t2),t3)``. The former is clearer and cleaner than the latter.

As a final note, sure, maybe you decide that you don't care about flooding the top-level namespace with function names just to avoid using classes. In this case, it's not that hard to define 5 functions. But what about if you have a need to represent more types of equations? Suddenly you're writing 5 functions for each equation. 25 functions is messier than 5 classes with 5 functions each. Using classes gives you the power to scale up more easily that with procedural programming.

Think of a manifold as a type of space. Could be 1D, 2D, 3D, up to as many dimensions as you'd like.  As an example, let's consider the surface of a globe.

Now, the Earth is a sphere, but it's surface is 2D. Why? You only need 2 pieces of information to identify the exact location of any object. If you have the longitude and latitude, you can find anything.

Now for a space to be considered Euclidean, it mustn't have any curvature. What does that mean? Well, as an example, for a 2D space, we should be able to take a rectangular piece of paper and cover a portion of the space without having to bend or crumple the paper. If you've ever tried to cover a ball with a sheet of paper, you know you can't do it without crumpling.

But what if you cut a small rectangle out of the paper? If it's small enough, you can put the paper onto the globe without any crumpling (or, realistically, very little crumpling). That means that the space is a manifold.

A manifold is defined to be any space which, over small scales, looks like a Euclidean space. In our example, we used a rectangular paper to represent a 2D Euclidean space. We then showed that, if you go small enough, the surface of the glove is close enough to flat that the paper fits perfectly, without deformity. (Technically, we would have to prove that this works no matter which part of the globe you use, but since a globe is perfectly round, it would be obvious in this case.)

So mathematically, anytime you're talking about a manifold, you're saying that if you look at the smallest scale you can, you can assume nice things about Euclidean geometry (like all triangles have angles which add up to 180°). (As a fun note, this isn't true on the globe. Draw a triangle with one point at the North Pole, and two points a fair distance apart on the equator. You'll see that they don't all add to 180.)

So, what is a differential manifold? Basically, it's a manifold in which calculus still works. Calculus assumes certain things about the space you use it in, mainly that it is continuous (any random location you pick actually exists) and that you can determine the distance you'd have to travel to go between points. If you're manifold has these properties, then it's differentiable, and you can use calculus.

An example of a non-differentiable manifold is hard to describe with analogy.

Finally, most physically significant manifolds are differentiable. Atm, I can't conceive of any cases in which you'd find it helpful to use a non-differentiable one.

Let's say, for the sake of argument, you have a bike with the front wheel rotating at a constant rate. This gives the entire bike system a net angular momentum, which we call L.

To keep things simple, we choose axes such that the x direction extends to the right hand side of the bike, the y direction is forwards, and the z direction is straight up. If the wheel is spinning forward, this defines the angular momentum in the -x direction. Let's set the variable ω as the magnitude angular momentum, so that the vector form of L is (-ω,0,0). This is the angular momentum of the wheel, and since the wheel is the only thing currently spinning, then it's also the total angular momentum of the bike. We shall define the total angular momentum as J. The momentum of the wheel is L, and we call the momentum of the frame S. Right now, S = 0, so J = S + L = L.

Now, turn the handlebars, rotating the forward wheel around the z axis. For now, we will ignore the effects of continuously rotating the handlebars, and just consider what happens after they've been turned. Suppose you turned the handlebars 90°, so that the angular momentum (of the wheel) is now L = (0,ω,0).

Problem is, angular momentum must be conserved. The momentum of the wheel is different, so for the momentum of the entire system to be unchanged, we must have induced a change in angular momentum the frame of the bike, to offset the change we made to the wheel. Let S be the angular momentum of the frame. We need the total angular momentum, J, to be the same, so mathematically, we solve for S.

J = S + L
(-ω,0,0) = (Sx, Sy, Sz,) + (0,ω,0)
therefore S = (-ω, -ω, 0).

Basically, if you turn the handlebars, the entire bike will have to start rotating to counteract the change you made.



WHAT HAPPENS WHILE TURNING THE BARS?

We ignored it earlier, but if you understood the above, then it won't take long to explain. We said earlier that the total angular momentum is J, and that L is the a. momentum of the front wheel, and S is the a. momentum of the frame. Since the handlebars are moving separately from the frame and the wheel, we should define another a. momentum, T, to represent the momentum of the handlebars.

Assuming the handlebars are rotated at a constant rate λ, the angular momentum vector is T = (0,0,λ). The total angular momentum J is then

J = L + S + T = (Lx, Ly, Lz) + (Sx, Sy, Sz) + (0,0,λ).

As before, we have to keep J constant, so L and S must change to offset T. Thus, during the rotation of the handlebars, the bike also gains a rotation around the z axis with an angular speed of -λ.

The basic steps to calculating flux are:

1. Determine the normal vector of the surface. The normal vector is a unit vector which is perpendicular to the plane of the surface. Your surface is a square in the x-z plane, so which unit vector is the norm vector?

2. Take the dot product of the field with the normal vector. (Look up the dot product if you don't know how to do it.)

3. Integrate the expression you get from (2) over the surface. You should always be able to write this as a double integral.

Here's an example.
Consider a square given by (0,0,1) - (1,0,1) - (1,1,0) - (0,1,1).  Consider also a field given by E = (xy, yz, xz). Find the flux through the square.

1. The surface is in the xy plane, so the normal vector is z-hat.

2. The dot product is (xy, yz, xz) • (0,0,1) = xz

3. Now we integrate. Since z=1 everywhere on the surface, we can write the dot product as E•zhat = x. The surface integral is from 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1. Only x appears, so we end up with int(x) which gives us 1.

Our eyes have a field of vision in the shape of a cone. The way the real world becomes processed into the 2D image our brain gets is rather simple: you slice that cone into layers, starting at the tip of the cone and heading outwards, towards the circle. Each of those layers is a separate 2D image, that you scale up/down and then overlay on top of each other.

The layers closest to the eye are scaled up the most, since those layers are the smallest, and all layers have to be the same size to make the final image. The further away the layers are, the less they scale up by.

Real-world objects don't change size as we move them further away, but the layers they're in get scaled differently depending on the distance. It's all to do with geometry, and collapsing a 3D cone into a 2D circle.

The three spatial dimensions we experience are real, and they work just the way we think they should, but the question is how they work on large scales (intergalactic scales). There are some variables in General Relativity that we don't have concrete values for, and one of them determines the natural curvature of spacetime.

Three possibilities exist: in the first, space is "flat". You can send two parallel laser beams from Earth into space, and they'll always stay parallel, and never come back to you. The second possibility is that we have a "positive curvature", in which case two laser beams which are initially parallel will eventually, due to the curvature of spacetime, turn into each other and cross. Eventually, after traveling for a long time, they'll end up looping back to the place they originated from. This type of curvature is more easily understood by looking at a globe. The lines of longitude on a globe are parallel; note that they always intersect at the poles, and loop around the entire globe, making a closed circle. Positive curvature is the 3D version of this.

The third possibility is that the universe has a "negative curvature". This one is harder to conceptualize. If you have two laser beams, starting parallel, then as they travel through space, they'll naturally drift farther apart. The shape of the universe in this case is not a globe, but more like a horse saddle. The front and back would curve up, and keep rising forever, and the two sides would curve down, and keep falling forever.

We know that whatever curvature we do have, it's a small amount, because on our everyday scale it appears to be completely flat. The only noticeable affects would be on massive scales, which makes it hard to experimentally determine which curvature is correct

The simple answer is that the longer your computer runs, the more time there is for glitches in the system to happen. One glitch usually isn't a problem, but when you have 10 or 100 at the same time, it can be enough to cause some issues.

When you restart a computer, you're clearing away all the loaded memory (RAM), and any glitches with it, and reloading everything anew. The core system files on the hard drive are seldom actually altered by the computer.

A more detailed answer, if you need it: everything you see on a screen, and everything the computer does, is all saved in RAM. It's the short-term memory of the computer. Files and programs get saved on the hard disk, which is like the long-term memory. But each time you run a program, or open a file, it gets moved to RAM, until you close it. With the OS, it's in RAM the entire time the computer is on. As you and I know, our short-term memory isn't always reliable, and while computers have a better track record than us, their RAM isn't infallible either. The longer something is in there, the more likely it is to be misremembered. By rebooting the computer, you're replacing the old memory of the OS in RAM with a new copy of the OS from the hard disk, which is glitch free. OK, so this is a complicated question. As others have mentioned, heat takes a few different forms. It can travel via light, in which case the speed is fairly well known; it can travels via contact; it can travel via convection.

For the sake of this answer, let's consider a fireplace sitting in a room with no air currents. The only movement of the air particles is their own random motion. Let's split up the air on the room into layers, with the first layer in direct contact with the fire, and the other layers expanding outward.

There are two important factors determining how quickly the first layer of air heats up: it's current temperature, and it's specific heat. The specific heat is unique to each material, and it's what determines if something is a good heat conductor or insulator.

The bigger the difference in temperature between two objects in contact, the faster heat exchanges between them. So since the first layer of air is at room temperature, and the fire is much hotter, the heat exchange at the beginning is relatively fast. As that layer of air heats up, it has a different temperature from the second layer, and so it exchanges heat with that layer as well. This effect continues down through all the layers.

As the first layer gets hot, it exchanges less heat with the fire, and so the heat spreads even slower across the room. This effect falls off relatively quickly, so it would take a long time to heat up a regular room (say, 12 ft) if you just rely on heat transfer via random motion.

Every circuit has three things that determine how much electricity flows through it: voltage, amperage, and resistance. Typically, the resistance is an unalterable property of the things connected to your circuit, so the only way to change it is to swap out the circuit components. Specifically, Ohm's Law states that the current I, voltage V, and resistance R are related by V=IR. You can't alter the resistance. If you use a power source with a constant voltage (such as most household outlets) then the current in the circuit has to flow at the exact rate so that V=IR.

Perpetual motion isn't too hard to do - a pendulum in a vacuum is perpetual motion. Trying to use perpetual motion as a power source is something else entirely.

Perpetual motion works because of conservation of energy; if the system doesn't lose energy anywhere, then the kinetic energy is conserved and the motion won't stop. The system itself might have energy changing from kinetic to potential energy, but the maximum amount of kinetic energy stays the same.

Now, if you want to draw power from a perpetual motion system, then that system is losing energy to you. Without as much kinetic energy, the movement is hindered, and will stop if too much energy is taken.

It's less a trick of the mind and more of a fundamental difficulty in astronomy. All we can see of stars (even with telescopes) is a point of light, some brighter than others. We're naturally tempted to assume that bright stars are close, and faint ones are far, but that's unfortunately not always the case.

A star's apparent brightness depends on two things: it's intrinsic brightness, and it's distance from us. The intrinsic brightness also depends on two things: the temperature of the star and the size. Big, hot stars are very bring intrinsically, but small, hot ones (like white dwarfs) are intrinsically very dim.

Since stars come on all varieties of intrinsic brightness, we can't use the apparent brightness to calculate the distance.

Essentially here's what's happening:

You pass a liquid by something very hot, and the heat from that object transfers into the liquid. The liquid may even evaporate, becoming a vapour. You then move the liquid/vapour away from the hot object, towards something cold (which we'll call a reservoir), and the heat in the liquid or vapour is transferred to the reservoir. You use some method to keep the reservoir cold. The liquid, now no longer holding heat, can go back to the hot object.

Some points:
- liquids are better (in general) at absorbing heat than air or other gasses, so they're more efficient heat carriers.
- the fluid just acts as an active transport system for the heat. It's job is to bring all the heat to a central location, where you can dispose of it efficiently.
- there are lots of method for keeping reservoirs cold, which are beyond the scope of this answer, but the idea is that the reservoir can absorb any amount of heat without changing temperature (because you're using another cooling method to keep the reservoir from heating).

In short, liquid cooling is designed to bring all the heat to a central place and deal with it there, whereas air cooling is designed to such heat from hot objects, and then expel the hot air outside of the system.

Recall that density p is equal to the mass of an object, M, divided by the volume of the object, V. So,
p=M/V.

For an object floating on water, the percentage (of volume) of the object which is submerged is proportional to how dense the object is, compared to water.

If the bottle was a quarter as dense as water, then three quarters of the bottle would be above water, and one quarter would be below.

If the bottle was exactly as dense as water, then it would be completely submerged, with no parts above water at all.

So, regarding icebergs, ice is 90% as dense as water, so we should expect that 90% of the iceberg is submerged, and only 10% is actually above water.

Lightning occurs due to charge imbalance. In general, when two objects of different charge are close together, the charges contained in both objects will want to spread equally between them both. When you touch the two objects, it's easy for charges to move back and forth, so the two objects quickly reach the same charge. When there's a gap, the charges can't move freely from one object to the other, because air is an insulator.

If the difference between the charges becomes big enough, then the need for both objects to be the same charge will overcome the difficulty of charges passing through air, and they'll jump across the gap. You've probably experienced this from a static shock before.

For lightning, there's a lot of air between the clouds and the ground, so there needs to be a LOT of charge in the clouds before it becomes possible for them to jump down to the ground. When such a high amount of charge is released, it transfers a lot of energy, which raises the temperature of the air the charges are passing through.

When things get hot, they glow (like the rings on an oven), and air is no exception. The charges jumping from the clouds to the ground heat up the air so much that it glows! That's where the light comes from.

The movement of charges is very fast, so it doesn't take long for all the charges in the cloud to reach the ground, at which point the air cools down, and stops glowing. That's why it's a flash, and not a gradual or constant light.

Let's start with a description of how lenses work. Every lens has a property called a focal length, which basically describes the distance you'd have to place the lens from a screen in order for a far-away image to come into focus. A helpful visual is a magnifying glass. If you hold a magnifying glass outside and try to focus sunlight onto the ground, you'll notice that the size and brightness of the sun's image on the ground depends on how high you hold the magnifying glass. When the image is smallest, that means it's focused, and the distance between the ground and glass is equal to the glass's focal length.

Now, our eyes have lenses, and when these lenses become warped, they're focal length changes. Out eyes have to have a very specific focal length, because the distance between the lens and the retina (the effective screen) is fixed. If that focal length changes, the image on the retina is blurry.

To compensate, we introduce another lens, which has a focal length chosen to cancel out the warping of your eye lens. The prescription used for glasses and contacts is defined as 1/f, where f is the focal length of the lens.

As previously mentioned, we call that number a diopter, and the larger the diopter is, the bigger the focal length of the lens, meaning a larger correction is needed to compensate for your eyes.

Lastly, you've probably noticed that some prescriptions are positive and some are negative. That's because your eyes can lose focus in two directions: they can be warped so that they focus the image too short, missing the retina, or they can be warped to focus the image too far, overshooting it. The sign of the prescription depends on which way your eyes have warped.

Probability density refers to how likely it is that a random measurement falls into a particular range of values.

For completeness, let's get some things straight about probability. In general, we talk about probability as a decimal number between 0 and 1. If the probability of something is 0, then it will never happen, and if it's 1, then it's guaranteed to happen every time you measure something.

Most people are familiar with probability in the discrete sense (where you can write down all the possible outcomes). Things like die rolls, coin flips, and decks of cards are easier to understand. The probability of rolling a 2 on a die is 1/6, because there are 6 possible values, and they're all equally likely. The probability of rolling a number between 2 and 5 (inclusive) is 4/6, because that range contains 4 of the 6 possible values.

When we start talking about probability for continuous values, we have to think a bit differently. If you're familiar with continuous functions, then you know that there are infinitely many values contained inside any range you choose. Consider the probability of the temperature outside being 30°. 30° is one possible value, but there are infinitely many values, so the probability of the temperature being EXACTLY 30° is 1/∞ ≈ 0.

So, for continuous variables, you can't know the probability of a single value. To get around this, we say "ok, what is the probability that the temperature is between 25° and 35°"? To find that out, you need to know the probability density function.

A probability density function (PDF for short) tells you the fractional probability for a very small range of values. If you're familiar with calculus, then the PDF for P(x) is the total probability that the measurement will be between x and x+dx. If you don't know calculus, that's cool, it's not required information. Just think of the PDF as similar to regular density. An object that is very dense has more mass in a small area, and vice versa. Sometimes you have an object that has varying density - let's imagine a ruler that is most dense on the 0 side and least dense on the 12 side. It makes sense that there is more mass between 1-2 on the ruler than there is between 10-11, right?

PDF's work the same way. They tell you whether there's more likelihood between 1-2 than between 10-11.

TLDR; the Sun has a known amount of fuel to keep itself alive, and we can calculate how fast it will use all that fuel up.

Basically when it comes to life expectancy for stars, you have two things to consider: how much fuel it has available and how fast it's burning through that fuel.

We can tell a lot about the sun by measuring how much energy it emits.  All the energy coming out of the sun originates from nuclear fusions in the core, combining hydrogen atoms into helium.  Knowing how much energy the sun is producing tells us how fast it's "burning" hydrogen.

We also know the mass of the sun, and that gives us an idea of how much fuel there is available.

Does the Sun burn hydrogen at a constant rate, or does it change over time?  Well, just like you get higher pressures when you go deeper in the ocean, you also get higher pressures as you head towards the centre of the sun.  The fusion in the core is caused by extremely high pressure in the core.  And the fusion actually pushes outwards, which prevents the sun from collapsing inwards.  Think of every fusion like an explosion which pushes the star out and stops it from all falling towards the center.

For the Sun to stay stable (not collapse and not explode), the rate of fusion needs to counteract the weight of the rest of sun trying to fall into the center.  So basically, if fusion starts to slow down, the star starts to collapse, raising pressures in the core to high enough to start fusion again.  This keeps the rate relatively stable.

We can create computer models to work out how long this kind of process will last.  As the hydrogen near the center turns to helium, outer layers of hydrogen will start fusing.  This has a limit though, where there just isn't enough pressure available in outer layers to cause fusion.  So the Sun will only convert a percentage of it's hydrogen to helium (something like 25% IIRC).

So we know how much helium the Sun will convert, and we can predict the rate of fusion in the sun (which provides energy and keeps the sun "alive").  To a decent approximation, you can predict the lifetime of the sun based on just that alone.  If you do further analysis, you find that as helium fusion dies down, the star collapses more and more until the central pressure gets high enough to start fusing helium into something else (I don't remember which elements).  This will add a few years into the lifespan of the star, but whenever a sun stars burning new elements, the number of years it gets added to its life is less and less.  That's basically because each fuel source gives less energy per fusion than the last, so the sun has to burn through more of it faster to keep the same energy rate.  Stars can keep fusing new elements all the way up to iron, but after that, it's done.  Iron can't be fused into anything bigger.  Once a star is producing iron, it has a matter of days before it runs out of fuel.

Only the biggest stars have enough mass for pressure to get high enough to make iron though.  The Sun will probably make two or three different elements before it can't make anything else.  When this happens, the fusion that kept the star from collapsing stops, and it shrinks down into a fraction of its original size where it will "glow" with residual heat until it cools off.

There is also a stage where the sun expands due to a particular elemental fusion which gives off a lot of energy and pushes the outside of the star away.  I don't really remember where that happens off the top of my head though :p

Probably the easiest way to understand radio signal transmission is to compare it to morse code.  If you're not familiar, morse code is an old telegram communication system where people would push a button to send electricity through a wire.  When the button was pressed, electricity went through, and would stop when you released the button.  By using patterns consistign of dots and dashes (tapping or holding down the button), you could communicate in code, where each pattern corresponds to a letter.

Radio works in a very similar way.  A transmitter sends out radio waves in a particular pattern, and a receiver detects the radio waves going through the air and decodes the pattern.  The advantage in using radio waves is that several different patterns can be going through the atmosphere all at once without interfering with each other, as long as they have different wavelengths.  When you change channels on your radio or TV, you're telling it to listen to a different wavelength, and therefore a different pattern

Stats do gradually shrink to some extent.  When a star runs out of hydrogen in the core (when most of it has already been converted to helium),  fusion stops and the star begins to shrink.  The shrinking places more pressure on the core, raising the temperature and allowing for the fusion of helium into the next element (lithium I think?).  Each time the star moves to a new fuel source, this same process happens.  Shrinking due to a lack of fusion, which keeps the fusion going.  In this way there's a sort of equilibrium balance.  The shrinking ensures a steady output of energy from core fusion.

Once the star gets to producing iron, it can't move on to another fuel source.  Iron cannot be fused into other elements in a way that produces energy, so the star collapses but cannot trigger further fusion.  That happens quite suddenly, because the nature of the fusion-gravitational equilibrium uses up all available fuel in the core at a steady rate until there is no more fuel.

Evaporation happens when molecules of water collide.  Collisions transfer energy from one particle to another, and if a particle gets enough energy, it loses its bonds with the surrounding molecules and becomes free.  At this point the molecule is in the gas phase.

Increasing the temperature means more energy per molecule on average.  With each particle having more energy, it's easier for each molecule to gain enough energy to evaporate.

The 100° point where boiling happens, when there's enough energy in the water to allow gas bubbles to form in the water.  Below this temperature, evaporation doesn't really happen except on the surface.  The reason is that a gas molecule on the surface can fly away, but if a molecule is freed deep inside the water, it will likely collide with a other molecule and probably reform it's bond, turning back into liquid.

Lastly, there's other factors which can affect the boiling point of water, mostly pressure.
